h1: The 8 Best 36V Leaf Blowers of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 cordless leaf blowers in the 36V class compared on airflow, battery platform, weight and kit contents, from Makita to EGO.
summary: The Makita XBU02PT is the best 36V leaf blower: a complete kit with batteries, 473 CFM and no gas. The EGO at 880 CFM is the pick for large yards and wet leaves. Makita owners should buy the bare XBU02Z, while the Mayoki is the cheap dual-battery option if compatibility checks out. The 18V picks suit small jobs.
intro: A 36V badge on a cordless blower does not mean what most buyers assume. Makita reaches 36V by running two 18V batteries side by side in one tool, so you are really buying into an 18V platform with a second pack. Other makers get comparable muscle from their own single-pack systems. Voltage alone tells you very little, and listings seldom state either airflow or runtime plainly.

We reviewed eight cordless blowers from their listings: three 36V-class tools from Makita and Mayoki, two EGO models and three single-18V picks as lighter alternatives. Each was scored on the Primea framework for airflow, kit contents, weight where stated and platform value. Where a listing never says 36V, we say so instead of assuming.

products.name: Makita XBU02PT 36V (18V X2) LXT Brushless Blower Kit
products.verdict: A complete 36V kit with batteries and charger, 473 CFM and zero gas to manage.
products.description:
Makita's XBU02PT is the 36V (two 18V) brushless blower sold as a complete kit, with batteries and charger in the box. It lists 473 CFM and zero emissions, with no gas, oil or pull cord. A brushless motor wears slower than a brushed one, because there are no carbon brushes to burn down, which matters on a tool you will run every autumn.

It wins because it works out of the box. The XBU02Z below is the same blower without packs, and the Mayoki leaves you hunting for batteries. The EGO 880 CFM pushes more air, but it asks for a separate platform and a heavier outlay.

Buy it for an ordinary suburban property and a battery platform you will keep. The caveat is price: the kit costs more than the bare tool, and it moves less air than the EGO.
cons: Kit costs more than the bare tool
products.idealFor: Homeowners who want a ready-to-use 36V blower.

products.name: EGO Power+ Cordless Electric Leaf Blower (880 CFM)
products.verdict: Up to 880 CFM and a turbo mode reaching 200 MPH. The strongest here by far.
products.description:
EGO's 880 CFM blower is the strongest machine here by a clear margin. The listing claims up to 880 CFM, and a turbo mode reaching 200 MPH, in a handheld body. Both numbers matter: volume clears piles, and speed peels up wet, caked leaves that a lower-speed blower just slides across the lawn.

It ranks second, not first, because it is the dearest pick in the $200 to $500 tier and the listing never states that it is a 36V tool. It also runs on EGO's own battery platform, so a Makita household gains nothing from existing packs. Against the Makita XBU02PT it moves far more air.

Buy it for big yards or wet, heavy debris. Skip it if you already sit on a Makita or Milwaukee platform, because starting a second battery family costs real money.
products.idealFor: Large yards and wet, heavy debris.

products.name: Makita XBU02Z 36V (18V X2) LXT Brushless Blower
products.verdict: The tool-only XBU02Z with a 6-stage velocity dial and a 61 dB(A) sound rating.
products.description:
The XBU02Z is the bare-tool version of Makita's 36V brushless blower. It lists a 6-stage air velocity dial and a 61 dB(A) sound rating under the ANSI B175.2 standard, in the $200 to $500 tier. The dial gives you a gentle setting for gravel borders and full power for matted leaves.

It ranks third because you must supply two 18V batteries and a charger, which the XBU02PT kit already contains. For someone with LXT packs in the garage that makes it the cheapest route to 36V, and for a newcomer the most expensive. The listing also gives no CFM figure, so you cannot compare its airflow with the EGOs.

Buy it if you own two 18V LXT batteries. Skip it if you are starting from nothing, and take the kit.
products.idealFor: Makita owners who already have batteries.

products.name: EGO POWER+ Cordless Electric Leaf Blower (530 CFM)
products.verdict: 530 CFM, suited to lighter cleanup rather than heavy wet debris.
products.description:
The 530 CFM EGO POWER+ is the mid-range sibling of the 880 CFM blower, in the $100 to $200 tier. It is a handheld cordless electric with no gas, no oil and no spark plug to maintain, which removes the seasonal tune-up that makes gas blowers tedious.

It ranks fourth because it moves far less air than the 880 CFM model and fits lighter jobs: dry leaves, grass clippings and driveway cleanup. Against the Makita XBU02PT it lists a little more airflow, but the EGO's platform is its own, so the saving shrinks if you need to buy batteries separately.

Buy it for small to mid-size lawns. Skip it if you face heavy wet leaf drifts, where 530 CFM stalls on soggy piles and the 880 CFM unit is worth the premium.

products.name: Mayoki Cordless Leaf Blower Compatible with Makita 18V Battery
products.verdict: A dual-battery design with 570 CFM that uses Makita 18V packs. Cheap for Makita owners.
products.description:
The Mayoki is a dual-battery cordless blower designed to run on Makita 18V packs, giving 36V-class output. It lists 570 CFM, three speeds plus Turbo, and a mid-mounted motor for a balanced center of gravity, in the $50 to $100 tier.

It ranks fifth because the tool is unbranded and works with Makita batteries by compatibility, not by Makita's design, so we cannot confirm how cleanly it handles them. On paper it lists more airflow than the XBU02PT and costs far less, but batteries are not included. That caveat decides everything: the saving only exists if you already own two LXT packs.

Buy it if you hold Makita batteries and want cheap power. Confirm compatibility with the seller before ordering, and skip it if you want a first-party warranty behind the tool.
products.idealFor: Makita battery owners who want cheap power.

products.name: Milwaukee M18 FUEL 120 MPH 450 CFM 18-Volt Lithium Ion Brushless
products.verdict: A single-18V brushless handheld with 450 CFM and 120 MPH. Fits the M18 ecosystem.
products.description:
The Milwaukee M18 FUEL is a single-18V brushless handheld that lists 450 CFM and 120 MPH, in the $100 to $200 tier. FUEL is Milwaukee's brushless line, and the tool slots into the wider M18 battery family.

It ranks sixth because it is a single-pack tool, not 36V, and it moves slightly less air than the 473 CFM Makita kit. A single pack means less power on tap and shorter runs than the dual-battery picks. Its case is platform loyalty: if your garage already runs on M18 batteries, you get a capable blower without a second battery system.

Buy it if you own M18 packs and have a typical yard. Skip it if you are choosing a platform from scratch, because a 36V-class tool offers more headroom for the money.
cons: Less airflow than the Makita kit

products.name: Makita XBU03Z 18V LXT Lithium-Ion Brushless Cordless Blower
products.verdict: A single-18V Makita with 459 CFM, an in-line fan and a speed lock.
products.description:
The Makita XBU03Z is a single-18V brushless blower that lists 459 CFM, an in-line fan design and a speed lock for continuous operation. The in-line fan keeps the weight along the axis of your arm, which reduces wrist strain, and the speed lock saves holding the trigger.

It ranks seventh because it is not a 36V tool, and the XBU02PT gets about the same CFM with more headroom from two batteries. It does cost less and runs on one pack, so a small property can live with it. Batteries are not included, which matters for the price comparison.

Buy it if you own one LXT battery and have a small lawn. Skip it for larger jobs, since a single pack runs down faster under load and you would need to step up to the XBU02PT kit.
products.idealFor: Small lawns with a single LXT battery.

products.name: Metabo HPT 18V Cordless Compact Blower
products.verdict: A 2.6 lb compact blower at the lowest cost. Only 124 CFM, so it is for light work.
products.description:
Metabo HPT's compact blower weighs 2.6 lbs and lists 124 CFM, in the $50 to $100 tier. It belongs to the MultiVolt battery family and is an 18V tool.

It ranks last because 124 CFM is a fraction of anything else here. For comparison, the Milwaukee lists 450 CFM and the Mayoki 570 CFM. That is not enough to move a lawn full of leaves. It wins on weight and cost, and the weight is real: at 2.6 lbs you can hold it overhead without fatigue.

Buy it for patios, decks and workshop sweeps where light dust and clippings are the target. Skip it if you clear leaves from a lawn, because the airflow figure is too low to do the job and you will end up raking by hand anyway.
products.skipIf: You clear leaves from a lawn.

methodology.title: 36V-class power
methodology.description: We ranked true 36V and dual-battery tools first, and marked single-18V tools as lighter alternatives.

methodology.title: Airflow on paper
methodology.description: CFM and air speed were compared where listings state them.

methodology.title: Kit contents
methodology.description: Bare tools and kits differ in cost, so batteries and chargers were counted.

methodology.title: Platform lock-in
methodology.description: Battery platform matters over years, so compatibility with wider tool lines was weighed.

methodology.title: Value in the field
methodology.description: Each tool was weighed against its price tier relative to the other seven.

whatMatters.detail: Makita's 36V tools run two 18V batteries together, while other brands use their own single-pack platforms. Comparing voltage tells you little, so compare stated CFM and runtime instead. Look for the words 18V x2 or dual battery on the listing, and note that the EGO listing here never states 36V at all.

whatMatters.factor: Check what is in the box
whatMatters.detail: Makita sells the same blower as a bare tool and as a kit with batteries and a charger. For a new buyer the kit is almost always cheaper than buying two packs separately, since the batteries are the costliest part. Read the box contents on the page before ordering, as the XBU02Z and Mayoki do not include batteries.

The battery is the expensive part, so choose a platform whose other tools you might buy: Makita LXT, Milwaukee M18, EGO or Metabo HPT MultiVolt. A cheaper blower on the wrong platform can cost more once you add packs. Count the packs, chargers and tools you already own before comparing sticker prices.

CFM is air volume and MPH is air speed. Wet leaves need speed, large piles need volume, and a spec sheet that gives only one hides the other. Check both on the listing. Be careful with listings that give neither, as the Makita XBU02Z does, because you cannot judge its power from the page alone.

A blower with batteries aboard gets heavy over a long session. Mid-mounted motors and in-line fans, like the Mayoki's and the Makita XBU03Z's, improve balance, while light tools like the 2.6 lb Metabo HPT save your arm. If your sessions run past 20 minutes, weight and balance matter as much as CFM, so check weight on the page.

faq.a: Two 18V batteries run together in one tool to make 36V, which doubles the pack count you must charge. Makita uses this setup on the XBU02Z and XBU02PT, and the Mayoki works the same way using Makita 18V packs.

faq.q: Do I need to buy batteries separately?
faq.a: For the Makita XBU02Z and the Mayoki, yes, so budget for two 18V packs and a charger. The XBU02PT kit includes batteries and a charger, so it is the one to choose if you own no Makita packs.
The listing does not state it. EGO uses its own battery platform and packs, so treat the 880 CFM and 530 CFM models as separate from the Makita and Mayoki 36V-class tools.

faq.q: Is a single-18V blower strong enough for leaves?
faq.a: For small lawns and light leaf fall, yes. The Milwaukee M18 lists 450 CFM and the Makita XBU03Z lists 459 CFM, though dual-battery tools such as the XBU02PT have more headroom on bigger jobs.

faq.q: Will the Mayoki work with my Makita batteries?
faq.a: It is sold as compatible with Makita 18V packs, but it is not a Makita product. Confirm compatibility with the seller before buying, and expect no Makita warranty to cover the blower itself.

faq.q: How loud is the Makita XBU02Z?
faq.a: The listing states 61 dB(A) per ANSI B175.2. That figure comes from the listing, not our own measurement, and none of the other blowers here publish a comparable sound rating, so quiet-street shoppers have little else to compare.

finalTake: For most yards, the Makita XBU02PT kit is the 36V blower to buy: 473 CFM, batteries included and no gas to manage. The EGO at 880 CFM wins when the job is large or the leaves are wet. Makita owners should look at the bare XBU02Z, and the Mayoki if compatibility holds. Choose the battery platform first, since it decides the long-term cost.
